explanations.answer: The servants who stand in His house
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The psalm says, "Give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God." (Psalm 135:1-2) These are the folks who are already standing right there in His house. I like that, because showing up is half the job. The other half is not hitting snooze.

explanations.answer: The kings who rule the nations
explanations.explanation: Kings do show up in this psalm, but later, and they're not the ones getting the call. Verse 10 says the LORD "…slaughtered mighty kings…" so they're on the other side of the story. The ones called to give praise are "servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD." (Psalm 135:1-2) It's the people already standing in His house, crowns not required.

explanations.answer: The shepherds who watch the flocks
explanations.explanation: I get the pick, friend, shepherds are all over the Bible. But this psalm never mentions them. It calls "servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God." (Psalm 135:1-2) So the sheep can relax. This call goes to the folks standing in His house.

True! The psalm says, "Hallelujah, for the LORD is good…" (Psalm 135:3) That "for" is the psalm handing you the reason. It could have said "just do it," but it tells you why. I like a teacher who explains himself, and I'd know.

Not quite, friend. The psalm says, "Hallelujah, for the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely." (Psalm 135:3) So the reason is right there in the verse: He is good. The psalm gives the praise a reason and then keeps stacking up more of them.

That's it, baker! Here's the verse: "For the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession." (Psalm 135:4) The psalm calls Israel treasured, not tolerated, not put up with. TREASURED. That's the kind of word you'd want said about you.

Army sounds tough, I'll give you that. But the psalm doesn't use it here. It says the LORD chose "…Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession." (Psalm 135:4) Treasured is a warmer word than army, and it's the one the psalm picked.

Close, friend, but that's not the wording here. The psalm says the LORD chose "…Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession." (Psalm 135:4) Treasured possession is the phrase. It's the kind of thing you keep in a safe place, not a box in the garage.
Yes, above! The psalm writer says, "For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods." (Psalm 135:5) Not next to them, not in the lineup. Above ALL of them. Nobody is even close.

Beside would put Him in the lineup, friend, and the psalm won't do that. The writer says, "our Lord is above all gods." (Psalm 135:5) Above means nothing else is in the same class. I know, one little word, and it changes the whole picture.
Among sounds friendly, but it makes Him one of the crowd. The psalm says, "our Lord is above all gods." (Psalm 135:5) He isn't one of the crowd. He sits over it.

Careful, friend, it's the opposite. The psalm says, "The LORD does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths." (Psalm 135:6) The seas and their depths are named right there. So there's no corner of the ocean that's off limits to Him.

False is right! The psalm says the LORD does all that pleases Him "…in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths." (Psalm 135:6) The deep seas are on the list. No spot is too far down for Him.

True! The psalm says He "…brings forth the wind from His storehouses." (Psalm 135:7) Storehouses, like the wind is kept somewhere ready to go. Meanwhile I can't keep the flour from blowing all over my own counter.

It's in there, friend. Verse 7 says He "…generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses." (Psalm 135:7) So the wind is on the list right along with the clouds, lightning and rain.

Yes, firstborn. The psalm says, "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." (Psalm 135:8) This is a heavy part, friend, and I think it's worth slowing down for. The psalm is looking back at what the LORD did in Egypt.

Strongest is a fair guess, but it's not the word here. The psalm says, "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." (Psalm 135:8) It's a heavy part, so I'll keep it simple. The word is firstborn.

Not quite, friend. The psalm says, "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast." (Psalm 135:8) Firstborn, and both man and beast are named. It's a heavy verse, and the word the psalm uses is firstborn.

explanations.answer: Gave it to Israel as an inheritance
explanations.explanation: That's right! The psalm says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." (Psalm 135:12) An inheritance is a gift handed down, not something you earn at the register. The land went to His people.

Nope, the land didn't sit empty, friend. The psalm says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." (Psalm 135:12) It went to Israel, His people. Nobody was left holding a "for lease" sign.

Good guess, but the psalm goes another way. It says, "He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel." (Psalm 135:12) The land was a gift to Israel. No sand in the story at all.
Not this time, friend. The psalm says, "Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations." (Psalm 135:13) Through ALL generations, not just one. That's way past one.

False, and you're right. The psalm says, "Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations." (Psalm 135:13) All generations, one after the next. His name doesn't wear out.
Yes, compassion! The psalm says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." (Psalm 135:14) That's a tender word. I'll take it.

I see why wrath comes to mind after those earlier verses, friend. But here the psalm says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." (Psalm 135:14) For His servants, the word is compassion.

Contempt isn't in this verse, friend. The psalm says, "For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants." (Psalm 135:14) Compassion is the word, and that's good news for the servants.

That's right! The psalm says, "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men." (Psalm 135:15) People made them. Imagine a thing that needs YOU to make it, and then can't even speak.
It's the other way around, friend. The psalm says the idols are "…made by the hands of men." (Psalm 135:15) The idols didn't make anything. People made them.
No angels in this verse, friend. The psalm says, "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men." (Psalm 135:15) These came from human hands, plain and simple.

Careful there, friend. The psalm says the idols have "…ears, but cannot hear…" (Psalm 135:17) They've got the ears, but they don't work. So you could shout your whole prayer list at them and get nothing back.
False, you got it. The psalm says, "…they have ears, but cannot hear…" (Psalm 135:17) Ears on the outside, nothing on the inside. That's one expensive pair of decorations.

Yes! The psalm says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." (Psalm 135:18) After that list of mouths that can't speak and ears that can't hear, that lands hard. I'd say that's a warning worth hearing.

Silver and gold might make you think so, friend. But the psalm says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." (Psalm 135:18) Riches aren't mentioned. What happens is that they become like the idols.
Long life isn't what the psalm says here, friend. It says, "Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them." (Psalm 135:18) The result is becoming like the idols. Not a prize.
That's it! The psalm says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" (Psalm 135:19) Aaron's house comes right after Israel's. The roll call is just getting started.

Eli was a priest (1 Samuel 1:9), so I see the thinking, friend. But the psalm doesn't call his house here. It says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" (Psalm 135:19) Aaron is the name it uses.
Zadok is a good guess, friend, but he's not in this psalm. The psalm says, "O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD…" (Psalm 135:19) Aaron's house is the one called next.

True! The psalm says, "O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!" (Psalm 135:20) That last call goes to everyone who fears the LORD. The roll call ends with a door held wide open.

It's in there, friend. The psalm says, "O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!" (Psalm 135:20) After Levi, it calls everyone who fears the LORD. So the call reaches past the families named before it.
Yes, Jerusalem! The psalm says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion—He who dwells in Jerusalem." (Psalm 135:21) That's the last blessing before the closing Hallelujah. That's a good ending.

Bethel is a place Jacob named (Genesis 28:19), friend, but it's not in this verse. The psalm says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion—He who dwells in Jerusalem." (Psalm 135:21) Jerusalem is the one named.
Hebron is where Sarah died (Genesis 23:2), friend, but this psalm doesn't name it. It says, "Blessed be the LORD from Zion—He who dwells in Jerusalem." (Psalm 135:21) Jerusalem is the answer.
